passage:
At ten, Francis received a thick envelope of Diwali money from relatives and spent all of it in one afternoon on sweets and a toy. The next week, with his own pocket money down to ten rupees, he refused to spend even that on a pencil box. Payal, his older sister, noticed. "It's all just money, you know." Francis shrugged. "Gift money doesn't count."

At sixteen, he won a quiz voucher and used it up in a day on games, yet he guarded the cash he earned running errands for the neighbours, counting it twice before closing the tin.

At twenty, Francis got a bonus from his campus job and bought a pair of earbuds without a second thought. Walking home the same evening, he skipped the bus to save a couple of rupees. Seema, a flatmate, watched him arrive footsore. "You just spent the bonus on earbuds, and now you're walking to save a bus fare?" Francis laughed. "The bonus was extra."

qa.q: What did Francis spend the Diwali money on?
qa.a: Francis spent all of it in one afternoon on sweets and a toy.

qa.q: What do the three stages show about how Francis treats money from different sources?
qa.a: At ten gift money counted as free to spend while pocket money felt precious; at sixteen a quiz voucher went in a day while earned cash was guarded; at twenty a bonus was spent easily while a small bus fare was saved. Francis's mind sorts the same rupees into separate pots by where they came from.

qa.q: What might Francis have been feeling when he said, "Gift money doesn't count"?
qa.a: Francis probably felt carefree and a little defensive, sure the gift belonged to a different category from his own money.

qa.q: How could Payal help her brother notice how he sorts money, without lecturing?
qa.a: Payal could kindly point out that a rupee from a gift and a rupee from pocket money buy the same things, and ask Francis how he decides which feels spendable.

grounding: A boy sorts money into separate mental pots by source at ten, sixteen and twenty, spending windfalls freely while guarding earned money.
